name: Harvest robotics
summary: Vision-guided, often soft-gripper machines that try to pick ripe berries without bruising — an active R&D frontier, not proof a named company has deployed robots commercially.
what_is_it: Harvest robotics for berries is selective picking by a machine that locates fruit (cameras, depth, learned detectors) and then grasps or detaches it with a mechanism meant not to crush flesh. Research systems include university strawberry prototypes that combine 3D vision with soft grippers and leaf-clearing, blackberry perception stacks, and modular strawberry pickers published as academic systems. This is different from over-the-row shake-and-catch machines used on some process blueberry and caneberry acreage: those are mechanical harvest, not a humanoid or arm picker in a fresh clamshell row.
why_it_matters: Hand harvest is a labor and bruising constraint on fresh berries. Competitors and universities talk about robots because labor cost and availability are strategic. A press mention of a trial, a grant, or a demo video is not the same as commercial conversion of a farm.
how_evaluated: Research papers report detection accuracy, cycle time, harvest rate, and bruise rates under experimental conditions. Those numbers are not interchangeable across papers or with a grower's packout. Commercial evaluation would be whether a named operation runs the machine on a named crop and pack — which this page does not assert.
what_affects_it: Canopy architecture, fruit hiding in leaves, ripeness mix, weather, and whether the system is open-field or protected-culture table-top. Soft fruit (strawberry, ripe raspberry) is harder than firm process blueberry. Training systems that present fruit in a plane help both human and machine pickers.
how_to_interpret: Treat robotics coverage as current technical guidance that ages quickly. Do not read a university demo or an accuracy percentage as a Fact about a competitor's harvest method. Do not collapse this into machine-harvest suitability of a variety: a cultivar can be shake-harvestable and still have nothing to do with a vision-guided arm. Pair with harvest methods and, for caneberries, trellis/training.

sources.title: Robotic harvester uses AI vision and soft grippers to pick hidden strawberries
